title: Value realized line on the other 19 pages - Publish / Hold
linkLabel: Open one page with the line (Automate the Invisible)
summary:
Your answer "Yes - same format": the line is now on every remaining pattern page, staged on overnight-2026-11-17 (commit c25020e). Roles and figures come from the Pattern Value Statements deck; two roles max; no "hire you did not have to make" sentence. Patterns with no pay figure get the assign-your-own-value line, like The Night Shift.

**Also found:** that same sentence is still LIVE on four pages - The AI Operations Manager, Avoid AI Slop, Assemble the Team and Models Are Not Good at Everything - and in the Pattern Value Statements deck (slides 2, 29 and 31). I staged its removal from the four pages (commit 45110da) as a separate question. The deck is not touched.

**Judge the Outcome, Not the Craft:** the deck never named what stays with people; I wrote "Deciding whether it's good enough stays with you."

Screenshot: https://github.com/level5consulting/ai-success-patterns/blob/overnight-2026-11-17/records/shots-2026-11-17/value-automate-the-invisible.png

**Begin with the End in Mind:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend redoing work that drifted away from what you actually needed, at your own pay rates. For example, scoping the work before it starts is part of a management analyst's job, a role that pays a median of about $101,860 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. Deciding what's worth doing stays with you."

**Onboard, Don't Program:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend re-explaining your work to the AI and fixing answers that missed what it wasn't told, at your own pay rates. For example, bringing someone up to speed on how your business works is part of a trainer's job - training and development specialists are a role that pays a median of about $69,280 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. Your knowledge of the business stays with you."

**Test Adversarially:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend finding and fixing errors after the work has already gone out, at your own pay rates. For example, attacking work for errors before it ships is what a quality assurance tester does; BLS reports testers in one median with software developers, about $134,040 a year, which the developers pull up (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. Checking against real sources stays with you."

**AI as Amplifier, Not Foundation:** "Assign your own value here - your call, not hours times a rate. Think of what it's worth to you to defend every piece of work you hand in because you know it, not because the AI wrote it. There's no clean pay figure for this work, so we don't give one. The judgment it amplifies stays with you."

**Own the Thinking:** "Assign your own value here - your call, not hours times a rate. Think of what it's worth to you that your decisions and recommendations are still your own, and that you can explain every one of them. There's no clean pay figure for this work, so we don't give one. Your thinking stays with you."

**The Compressed Apprenticeship:** "Assign your own value here - your call, not hours times a rate. Think of what it's worth to you to have people who learn faster on real work, and who still know why when the AI isn't in the room. This pattern builds your people; it doesn't cover a role. There's no clean pay figure for this work, so we don't give one. Mentoring stays with people."

**The Productivity-to-Headcount Trap:** "Assign your own value here - your call, not hours times a rate. Think of what it's worth to you to keep the people who know the work when AI makes them faster. This pattern argues against cutting people after a productivity gain, so a pay figure would point the wrong way. There's no clean pay figure for this work, so we don't give one. Everything here stays with people."

**Automate the Invisible:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend on booking, confirmations, follow-ups and the rest of the admin that waits until Sunday night, at your own pay rates. For example, that is work an administrative assistant does - secretaries and administrative assistants are a role that pays a median of about $48,310 a year, and executive administrative assistants about $76,590 (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). Those are examples. Client-facing work stays with you."

**Embed the Expert:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours your expert spends answering the same questions again and again, at your own pay rates. For example, passing an expert's know-how on to others is part of a trainer's job - training and development specialists are a role that pays a median of about $69,280 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. The expert's judgment stays with the expert."

**The Staged Journey:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend planning an AI rollout stage by stage, and undoing a stage you skipped, at your own pay rates. For example, that planning is part of a management analyst's job, a role that pays a median of about $101,860 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. Leadership's choices stay with leadership."

**Right Tool, Right Job:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend comparing AI tools, and working around the wrong one, at your own pay rates. For example, matching the tool to the job is what a technology consultant does - the nearest match, computer systems analysts, is a role that pays a median of about $105,850 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. The buying decision stays with you."

**Avoid the Naughty List:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend checking AI work against your organization's rules, and cleaning up after a slip, at your own pay rates. For example, that check is part of a compliance officer's job, a role that pays a median of about $80,730 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. Legal and compliance sign-off stays with your qualified people."

**Research Partner, Not All-Knowing Oracle:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend finding, sorting and summarizing sources, at your own pay rates. For example, a market research analyst is a role that pays a median of about $78,760 a year, and a research assistant (social science research assistants) about $61,990 (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). Those are examples. Checking stays with you - you open every source and read the quote yourself."

**Iterate to the Destination:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend on rounds of drafting and revising, at your own pay rates. For example, those rounds are what a writer does - writers and authors are a role that pays a median of about $76,910 a year - and an editor about $77,920 (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). Those are examples. Knowing when it's done stays with you."

**Redesign the Stream, Not the Role:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend mapping how the work flows, where it waits and where it gets redone, at your own pay rates. For example, mapping a process is part of a management analyst's job, a role that pays a median of about $101,860 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. The process stays in the hands of the people who run it."

**Ten People, One Idea:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend running a session to pull different ideas out of a group, at your own pay rates. For example, that is a workshop facilitator's job - the nearest match, training and development specialists, is a role that pays a median of about $69,280 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. The ideas stay with the people who had them."

**AI Friction:** "Assign your own value here - your call, not hours times a rate. Think of what it's worth to you to spot the places where AI slows the work down or doesn't belong. There's no clean pay figure for this work, so we don't give one. Knowing when not to use AI stays with you."

**Dashboards That Answer a Question:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend building and reading reports that nobody acts on, at your own pay rates. For example, building a report that answers a real question is part of a business analyst's job - the nearest match, management analysts, is a role that pays a median of about $101,860 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. The decision stays with you."

**Judge the Outcome, Not the Craft:** "Insert your own savings numbers here. Count the hours you'd spend having someone check work you can't do yourself, at your own pay rates. For example, that is what an outside technical reviewer does - the nearest match, computer systems analysts, is a role that pays a median of about $105,850 a year (Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2025, pay only, not benefits). That is an example. Deciding whether it's good enough stays with you."
